question: Why do warmup-stable-decay and cosine learning-rate schedules for language-model training resemble last-iterate bounds from nonsmooth stochastic convex optimization, and can that resemblance guide tuning?

key_findings.claim: A last-iterate subgradient bound predicts the sharp benefit of cooldown and distinguishes constant-plus-linear-decay from cosine schedules.
key_findings.evidence: The bound depends on weighted step-size sums and nonvanishing gradient-norm bounds. Linear cooldown removes logarithmic terms that penalize the last iterate under a constant schedule, producing curves qualitatively similar to observed validation loss despite the model being nonconvex and trained with AdamW.

key_findings.claim: The theoretical optimum predicts that cosine should use about twice the base learning rate of WSD in the tested regime.
key_findings.evidence: Sweeps on 124M and 210M Llama-type models show the best cosine rate close to twice the best WSD rate, matching the schedule-dependent factor in the convex expression. This agreement is empirical and scale-limited, not a guarantee for arbitrary optimizer hyperparameters.

key_findings.claim: The bound is used to extend a training horizon and transfer tuned rates across schedules with measurable small-model improvements.
key_findings.evidence: For continued pretraining, adapted schedules improve validation loss by about 0.01; scaling-law estimates equate this to roughly 6-8% more tokens or 4-5% more parameters in the reported setups. A transferred full linear-decay run reaches 2.9535 versus 2.9660 for the best 20%-cooldown run.

key_findings.claim: The convex bound is a design heuristic, not an explanation of nonconvex large-model optimization.
key_findings.evidence: The limitations explicitly note that the theorem is an upper bound for convex nonsmooth objectives and omits architecture, data mixture, weight decay, and stability. The proposed account ultimately relies on gradient norms not going to zero, which may arise from nonsmoothness or stochastic noise but is not identified experimentally.

method.core_idea: Treat a tractable last-iterate convex bound as a surrogate laboratory for learning-rate schedule shape and rate transfer.
method.mechanism: Derive the bound for arbitrary schedules and WSD cooldown, use performance-estimation problems to assess tightness, compare its shape and optimal rate with Llama validation curves, and use its schedule factors to construct continued-training and cross-schedule recipes.
assumptions: Nonvanishing stochastic gradient norms dominate schedule behavior similarly in convex and deep-learning settings.
The bound's relative schedule dependence transfers even when its absolute assumptions fail.
Small Llama-type models and ImageNet SGD are informative about larger training.
Data order, optimizer moments, and weight decay do not overturn the schedule ratio.

techniques.role: Predicts cooldown benefit for nonsmooth stochastic optimization.
Checks upper-bound tightness against constructed worst cases.
Maps a tuned WSD rate to cosine or linear decay.
Designs a longer horizon while reusing stable-phase progress.

evaluations.setting: 124M and 210M Llama-type models on OpenWebText-style data
evaluations.metric: Validation loss across schedule and base-rate sweeps
evaluations.result: Bound shapes mirror cooldown drops and predict an approximately 2x cosine-to-WSD optimal rate
evaluations.baseline: Cosine, constant, WSD, and linear decay

evaluations.setting: Continued training to longer token horizons
evaluations.metric: Final validation loss and equivalent compute
evaluations.result: About 0.01 loss improvement, estimated as 6-8% additional tokens in matched scaling-law terms
2.9535 versus 2.9660 for the best reported 20% cooldown run

evaluations.metric: Qualitative loss shape and optimal-rate ratio
evaluations.result: The cosine/WSD factor and schedule-shape pattern persist

limitations: Author-stated: the theorem applies to convex objectives, unlike deep networks.
Author-stated: the bound cannot match training curves exactly and omits many recipe variables.
Reviewer-identified: language experiments stop at 210M parameters, far below the title's broad large-model framing.
Reviewer-identified: rate sweeps and shared datasets can make qualitative agreement easier to find without out-of-sample prediction.
Reviewer-identified: the explanation for persistent gradient norms is left unresolved.
failure_modes: Optimizer moments make effective step sizes diverge from the scalar schedule.
Gradient norms decay or undergo phase transitions, invalidating the surrogate.
A changed batch size or token correlation shifts the optimal-rate ratio.
Continued training crosses a data or curriculum boundary.
The bound optimizes worst-case loss while downstream quality prefers another schedule.
Large-scale stability constraints cap the theoretically transferred rate.
reusable_insights: Use simple theory to propose schedule ratios prospectively, then test without retuning.
Separate shape prediction from absolute convergence guarantees.
Report optimizer-effective step sizes alongside nominal learning rates.
Validate schedule heuristics across scale, batch, data, and optimizer changes.
Translate small loss changes into compute only with uncertainty on scaling-law fits.
open_questions: Does the 2x rate-transfer rule survive billion- and tens-of-billions-parameter training?
Can AdamW moment dynamics be incorporated into an equally tractable bound?
What mechanism keeps gradient norms nonzero in language pretraining?
Can held-out schedule shapes be selected prospectively from the bound?
How do batch size, sequence length, and data repetition alter cooldown length?

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Warmup-Stable-Decay Learning Rates: A River Valley Loss Landscape Perspective
competitive_landscape.difference: Wen et al. explain WSD through fast progress along a valley and oscillation transverse to it, and propose WSD-S. The present paper instead uses a nonsmooth convex last-iterate bound and emphasizes learning-rate transfer.

competitive_landscape.title: Optimal Linear Decay Learning Rate Schedules and Further Refinements
competitive_landscape.difference: Defazio et al. derive and test linear-decay schedule theory. This paper extends the last-iterate comparison to WSD/cosine behavior and language-model tuning transfers.

competitive_landscape.title: Power Scheduler: A Batch Size and Token Number Agnostic Learning Rate Scheduler
competitive_landscape.difference: Power Scheduler aims for transferable schedules across token counts and batch sizes. The present method transfers rates through a convex surrogate but does not establish the same invariance across training regimes.

competitive_landscape.title: WSM: Decay-Free Learning Rate Schedule via Checkpoint Merging for LLM Pre-training
competitive_landscape.difference: WSM replaces explicit decay with checkpoint averaging and reports downstream gains over WSD. It is current competition to any claim that cooldown is operationally necessary, even if the convex bound explains why it helps the last iterate.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: A nonsmooth convex bound unexpectedly mirrors large-model schedule curves closely enough to design cooldowns, continued training, and cross-schedule learning-rate transfer.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper derives the bound, checks tightness, matches multiple qualitative patterns, and reports two small-model applications plus an ImageNet extension.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The useful novelty is the specific WSD last-iterate derivation and empirically successful rate-transfer heuristic. It is not a theory of nonconvex language-model training, and evidence at 124M-210M parameters makes larger-scale claims provisional.

reviewer_notes: Read all 28 extracted pages, including theorem, PEP checks, applications, explicit limitations, scaling-law conversion, ImageNet extension, and schedule appendix. Four primary arXiv competitors, including a later checkpoint-merging alternative, were checked on 2026-08-23. No training runs were independently reproduced.
